title: Static testing basics
body:
# What static testing is
**Static testing** examines a work product *without running it*. Nothing is executed: people read it (a **review**) or a tool checks it (**static analysis**).

You already do this. Reading the crafting section of a GDD and spotting that two recipes need the same unique item is static testing. So is a Roslyn analyzer warning you that a C# variable is never assigned.

**Exam trap:** "static testing = done by hand, no tools". Wrong. Static analysis is tool-driven and still static, because nothing runs.

# FL-3.1.1 (K1): what can be examined
Almost any work product you can read and understand can be examined statically:

- requirements, user stories and acceptance criteria
- designs and architecture (e.g. a networking design doc)
- source code (C# scripts, shaders)
- testware: test plans, test cases, test charters
- models, such as an Animator state machine graph
- project documents: plans, schedules, budgets, contracts
- user-facing text: manuals, help pages, store-page copy

Static **analysis** needs a work product with a formal structure a tool can check: code, models, or structured text.

**Not suitable:** work products that people cannot sensibly interpret *and* that you must not analyse with tools. Example: a closed-source middleware delivered only as compiled binaries, whose licence forbids decompiling.

**Exam trap:** "static testing is only for code". Wrong: requirements and test cases are classic review targets.

# FL-3.1.2 (K2): why it is worth it
- **Early detection.** Defects are found before any build exists, when fixing them is cheapest. A contradiction fixed in the level-design doc costs minutes; the same bug found after release costs a patch.
- **Defects dynamic testing cannot find.** Unreachable code, an unused variable, a design that ignores the agreed pattern, or a mistake in a document that is never executed at all.
- **Shared understanding.** A review gets designers, developers and testers to read the same requirement the same way, so fewer misunderstandings reach the code.
- **Quality evaluation and confidence.** Reviews show how good a work product is before people build on it.

Static **analysis** is often cheap too: no test cases are needed, and tools do most of the work.

Reviews cost time, but finding defects early usually makes the total cost of the project *lower*, not higher.

**Exam trap:** "static testing replaces dynamic testing". Wrong: the two are **complementary**.

# FL-3.1.3 (K2): static versus dynamic
Both aim to find defects and to evaluate quality. The key difference:

- **Static testing finds defects directly** (in the document or the code).
- **Dynamic testing causes failures**; someone must then analyse each failure to find the defect behind it.

Remember the chain from Chapter 1: error → defect → failure. Static testing works on the *defect* without ever seeing a failure.

Other differences worth knowing:

- Static testing can be used on work products that **cannot be executed** (a GDD, a test plan).
- Static testing can reach code paths that are **rarely or never executed**, which dynamic tests may miss.
- Static testing measures characteristics that do **not depend on execution**, such as **maintainability**. Dynamic testing measures those that **do**, such as **performance efficiency** (frame rate, load time).

Defects that are typically **easier to find statically**:

- requirement defects: contradictions, ambiguities, omissions
- design defects: poor modularisation, inefficient data structures
- some coding defects: undefined values, unreachable or duplicated code, excessive complexity
- deviations from standards, e.g. naming conventions
- wrong interface specifications (two teams assuming different units)
- some security vulnerabilities
- gaps in test basis coverage (an acceptance criterion with no test)

# Unity connections
- GDD crafting review before code exists = static testing on a non-executable work product.
- Analyzer warning on an unassigned field = static analysis finding a defect directly.
- Profiler run showing 40 FPS in the boss arena = dynamic testing: a failure to investigate.

# Side note for Chapter 6
A **static testing tool** supports reviews and static analysis (linters, code analysers, review features). A wiki or chat tool is a *collaboration* tool, not a static testing tool. This was one of your logged traps.

title: Feedback and the review process
body:
# Reviews in one minute
A **review** is static testing done by people: they read a work product and look for problems in it. Section 3.2 is about how reviews are run: why early feedback matters, the steps of a review, who does what, the four review types, and what makes reviews work.

**Exam trap:** review types are not test levels. "Walkthrough" and "inspection" sit next to "informal review" and "technical review", never next to "component testing" or "acceptance testing".

# FL-3.2.1 (K1): early and frequent stakeholder feedback
Getting feedback from stakeholders early, and again and again, has these benefits:

- **Potential quality problems are communicated early**, while they are still cheap to deal with.
- **Misunderstandings about requirements are prevented**, and **changes to requirements are understood and implemented earlier**.
- The team **understands what it is building** better.
- The team can **focus on the features that deliver the most value** to stakeholders and that have **the most positive impact on the identified risks**.

What happens without it: the product can drift away from what stakeholders had in mind. The result is **costly rework, missed deadlines, blame games** and, at worst, a failed project.

Game example: a studio sends its script outline to the localisation partner in month one and hears that three key jokes cannot be translated. Rewriting an outline is cheap; re-recording finished voice-over is not.

**Exam trap:** "feedback guarantees the product meets every stakeholder's expectations" or "approved features need no testing". Wrong: feedback lowers the risk of building the wrong thing; it proves nothing and replaces no testing.

# FL-3.2.2 (K2): the review process
The syllabus uses a generic process (based on ISO/IEC 20246) with five activities. The more formal the review, the more of it is followed in full.

1. **Planning.** Set the scope: the purpose, the work product, the quality characteristics to evaluate, areas to focus on, the **exit criteria**, supporting information such as standards, and the effort and time available.
2. **Review initiation.** Make sure everyone and everything is ready: participants can open the work product, know their roles and have what they need (checklists, standards).
3. **Individual review.** Each reviewer works *alone*, assesses the work product and logs **anomalies**, recommendations and questions, using a review technique such as checklist-based or scenario-based reviewing.
4. **Communication and analysis.** The anomalies are discussed, often in a review meeting. Each one gets a status, an owner and the action needed. The group also judges the quality of the work product and decides on follow-up, which can be another review.
5. **Fixing and reporting.** A **defect report** is created for every defect so the fixes can be followed up. When the exit criteria are met, the work product can be accepted, and the review results are reported.

Order check, with a skill-tree design: the lead sets the goal and exit criteria (planning) → sends the doc and checklist to four people (initiation) → each reads it alone and notes problems (individual review) → they meet and sort the notes into real defects and non-issues (communication and analysis) → the designer fixes, the bugs are tracked, the review closes (fixing and reporting).

**Exam trap:** "an anomaly is a defect". Wrong: an anomaly is anything that looks wrong; analysis decides whether it is a defect.

**Exam trap:** exit criteria are set in **planning**, not invented at the end.

# FL-3.2.3 (K1): review roles
- **Manager**: decides *what* is reviewed and provides the resources (people and time).
- **Author**: creates the work product and fixes it.
- **Moderator** (also **facilitator**): makes the review meetings work: mediation, time management, a safe place to speak.
- **Scribe** (also **recorder**): collates the reviewers' anomalies and records review information, such as decisions and new anomalies found in the meeting.
- **Reviewer**: performs the review. Can be a team member, a subject-matter expert or any other stakeholder.
- **Review leader**: has overall responsibility for the review, such as choosing who takes part and organising when and where it happens.

One person can hold more than one role, especially in less formal reviews.

**Exam trap (your logged one):** in an **inspection** the author **may not be the review leader or the scribe**. The author still *takes part*. "The author cannot review" or "the author leads" are both wrong.

**Exam trap:** manager vs review leader. The manager *decides what* and *gives resources*; the review leader *organises who, when and where*. The moderator runs the meeting itself.

# FL-3.2.4 (K2): the four review types
From least to most formal:

- **Informal review**: no defined process, no formal documented output. Main objective: detecting anomalies. Example: a colleague takes a quick look at your new bug-report template.
- **Walkthrough**: **led by the author**. It can serve many objectives: evaluating quality and building confidence, **educating reviewers**, gaining consensus, generating new ideas, motivating authors to improve, detecting anomalies. Reviewers *may* do an individual review first, but it is not required.
- **Technical review**: held by **technically qualified reviewers** and **led by a moderator**. Main objectives: **gaining consensus and making decisions about a technical problem**; also detecting anomalies, evaluating quality, building confidence, new ideas.
- **Inspection**: the **most formal** type. It follows the **complete generic process**. Main objective: **finding the maximum number of anomalies**. **Metrics are collected** and used to improve the SDLC, including the inspection process itself. The author cannot be review leader or scribe.

How to choose: by the needs of the project, the resources, the work product and its risks, the business domain and the company culture. One work product can get more than one review, e.g. an informal check of a draft, then a technical review.

Game examples, one per type:

- A writer asks a colleague to glance at a dialogue tree: informal review.
- The UI designer takes the localisation team through the new menu flow so they understand it: walkthrough.
- Senior engineers, with a moderator, decide how the save format should handle old versions: technical review.
- The age-rating questionnaire answers go through every step of the process, with defect metrics kept: inspection.

**Exam trap (your logged one):** "an inspection is a formal review". Not enough: it is the *most* formal, it follows the *full* process, it aims at the *maximum* number of anomalies and it collects *metrics*.

**Exam trap:** "the walkthrough is led by a moderator". Wrong: the author leads a walkthrough; a moderator leads a technical review.

# FL-3.2.5 (K1): what makes reviews succeed
- **Clear objectives and measurable exit criteria.** Evaluating the participants is **never** an objective.
- **The right review type** for the objectives, the work product, the people and the context.
- **Small chunks**, so reviewers do not lose concentration.
- **Feedback** from reviews to stakeholders and authors, so they can improve the product and their own work.
- **Enough time to prepare.**
- **Support from management.**
- Reviews as **part of the organisation's culture**, for learning and process improvement.
- **Training** for all participants.
- **Facilitated meetings.**

**Exam trap:** "use the review results to rate each author" sounds like accountability. It is the opposite of a success factor: people stop bringing their work to reviews.

# Unity connections
- A sprint-end demo to the publisher = early and frequent stakeholder feedback.
- Reading a quest doc alone with a checklist = individual review; the meeting after it = communication and analysis.
- Pull-request comments from the dev next to you = close to an informal review; the cert-compliance pass with metrics = an inspection.

# Side note for Chapter 5
The defect reports born in **fixing and reporting** are the same kind of report you will write in Chapter 5 (defect management).
